name: Ninkãrɛ
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Niggli, Idda & Urs Niggli. 2007. De la phonologie à l'orthographe: Le ninkãrɛ au Burkina Faso. Cahiers de Recherches Linguistiques de la SIL et l'ANTBA Burkina Faso, Numéro 10. Ouagadougou: Société Internationale de Linguistique. 130 pp. (open PDF, sil-burkina.org)
catalog_locator: §4.7.2 « L'accent d'intensité », p. 82; same rule restated in Niggli & Niggli 2007, Esquisse grammaticale du ninkãrɛ (Cahiers No. 11), §1.3.3, p. 26
catalog_quote: Certains segments sont accentués, ils ont l'accent d'intensité [']. Ces segments d'énoncé sont réalisés avec une intensité particulière sans que l'on puisse attribuer cette intensité à un effet d'insistance. 'Bʋraa la 'sɛ̃ŋɛ la 'Poogo. «L'homme est allé à Pô.» En ninkãrɛ, la place de l'accent d'intensité n'a aucune valeur distinctive. Cet accent marque automatiquement la première syllabe du mot phonologique sauf s'il s'agit d'un pronom ou d'une particule grammaticale. A 'sɛŋɛ la 'Poogo. «Il est allé à Pô.» L'accent d'intensité provoque un rehaussement du niveau mélodique du ton affectant la syllabe portant l'accent, ce ton est donc réalisé à un registre supérieur à celui de son registre normal (ton bas rehaussé B+ ou ton haut rehaussé H+). tìà est réalisé: 'tīà «arbre» [B B → B+B] ... fúúgó est réalisé: 'fúúgó «vêtement» [H H → H+ H]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Certain segments are accented; they carry the stress accent [ˈ]. These stretches of the utterance are realised with a particular intensity without this intensity being attributable to emphasis. [...] In Ninkãrɛ the position of the stress accent has no distinctive value. This accent automatically marks the first syllable of the phonological word, unless the word is a pronoun or a grammatical particle. [...] The stress accent raises the melodic level of the tone on the syllable bearing it, so that tone is realised in a register higher than its normal one (raised low B+ or raised high H+).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ninkãrɛ (Burkina Faso Farefare) is a two-tone (H/L, downstep) terraced-level tone language; in addition it has a non-contrastive intensity stress that falls automatically on the first syllable of every phonological word (nouns, verbs etc., e.g. ˈbʊraa, ˈsɛ̃ŋɛ, ˈPoogo, ˈtɪ̀à, ˈfúúgó), pronouns and grammatical particles being unstressed; the stressed syllable's tone is realised in a raised register.
new_statements.exceptions: Pronouns and grammatical particles do not receive the accent (e.g. subject pronoun a, determiner/particle la unstressed in 'A ˈsɛŋɛ la ˈPoogo'). Independent Ghana-side account (Kropp Dakubu 2006, as reported by Adongo 2018): accent on the first syllable of any lexical stem WITHOUT A PREFIX, i.e. prefixes are skipped; accented onsetless syllables take a glottal stop.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'mot phonologique' (phonological word) within connected utterances; examples are sentences, with stress marks on each lexical word. Stress is explicitly stated to be non-distinctive and to interact with tone (register raising), tone being the lexically contrastive prosody (though of low functional load, §4.8).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source describes Ninkãrɛ, the Burkina Faso variety of Farefare/Gurenne (speech of Guélwongo taken as the written standard; ca. 30,000 speakers in BF vs ca. 500,000 in Ghana), which the authors equate with gʋrnɛ/gurenne/nankana/frafra; Glottolog files these Niggli works directly under fare1241 (no separate dialect code assigned; closest Ghana-side dialect label is Nankani). The Ghana-side Gurenɛ (Bolgatanga) account by Kropp Dakubu 2006, known second-hand from Adongo 2018, agrees on initial accent but formulates it as the first syllable of the unprefixed lexical stem.

tone_statements.quote: the tonal status of Gurenɛ remains contested: some scholars describe it as a two-tone language, whereas others provide evidence for a three-tone system.
tone_statements.locator: quote verbatim in the abstract, p. 1 of 37 (also verbatim in the Crossref abstract); Gurenɛ section §3.3 pp. 16-19 of 37 (§3.3.1 Tone Inventory pp. 16-18, §3.3.2 Tonal Processes pp. 18-19)
tone_statements.summary: Lexical + grammatical tone; 2-tone (H, L, downstep) vs 3-tone (H, M, L) analyses in dispute.

sources.note: §4.7.2 'L'accent d'intensité' (p.82): stress placement has no distinctive value; it automatically marks the first syllable of the phonological word, except pronouns and grammatical particles; the stressed syllable's tone is realised in a raised register (B+ / H+). Tone chapter (p.67): two tonemes H and L with downstep; 'accent d'intensité' listed among factors modifying tone realisation.

sources.citation: Adongo, Helen Atipoka. 2018. Aspects of Gurenɛ Phonology. PhD thesis, University of Ghana, Legon.
sources.note: No stress analysis of its own (chapters on segments, syllable/mora, harmony, tone: 'Gurenɛ is a tone language with the mora as the TBU', two basic tones H/L with downstep, p.196). Literature review (pp.43, 225) reports Kropp Dakubu 2006: 'the first syllable of any lexical stem (noun, verb, adjective or adverb) without a prefix can carry accent', and an initial glottal stop is a function of accent.

tone.says: 'The aspects of Gurenɛ phonology discussed in this thesis are the phonemic system, the syllable, tone, harmony and other phonotactic processes.. the Autosegmental phonology was employed to analyse tonal and segmental processes.. The CV and CVC are the basic or core syllable types, while the mora is the tone-bearing unit in Gurenɛ.' Inventory: Atintono 2004 gives two contrastive tones H and L, realised on the syllable nucleus, with lexical minimal pairs in verbs (kóné 'knock' / kònè 'miss') and nouns (sánɛ́ 'melon' / sànɛ̀ 'debt', báŋá 'ring' / bàŋà 'lizard'); Adongo 2018 argues for three level tones H, M, L (láá 'bowl', dāā 'past', làà 'falling position') with contours HL/LH analysed as derived, i.e. a register-tone language; TBU = mora (Adongo).
